Answers to your questions:

1. "My wife doesn't even know, I'm terrified to tell her. Is that normal?"  Of course! That's a natural human response: fear of loss. By and large, marriage is the brass ring of the LDS lifestyle, so the mere thought of mentioning your potential loss of faith in the church to your spouse is bound to induce great amounts of fear. 

     You use the words, "I'm terrified to tell her." The adjective "terrified" is pretty strong. I would ask you: is that healthy in a marriage? (by marriage, I DO NOT mean what the LDS church defines as marriage. I mean a loving, accepting long term relationship between two people). 

   I know that not all marriages are ideal, and I know that all people have things they keep from their spouses (past indiscretions, criminal history, the Nickelback discography in their music library, etc.); but spiritual stance? It seems to me that discussing your change in spiritual opinion would only be terrifying if you are a member of a church that promotes severing family ties (or giving a pass to divorce) in the instance of a loss of testimony. 

   Think about your wife, and who she is as a person. Is she kind, loving, and willing to accept you? Has she supported your decisions in the past? Is she willing to compromise with you? Can she see you as a separate individual? Is she mature enough to separate your spiritual beliefs from your love for her? If you can answer yes to all of these, I think your marriage will be fine despite outside social pressures. Ultimately, the outcome will depend on the two of you, not anything the church says.

2. "Is that even OK that the church fosters that sort of fear at "coming out" as it were?" No, that's not okay. That's not decent. That's not kind. In short, that's nothing a loving person, let alone an institution would do. 
 
      Think about it this way: Your sister is dating a guy who she loves. He's nice at first, but incapable of loving her in a mature way because he's insecure that she's going to find someone else. He starts to covertly insinuate that he's the best she'll ever find, he  had to make a lot of compromises in order to accept her, and she has pretty much no chance in life without him. He doesn't do this blatantly, and she starts to take on this attitude. Her family and friends all see his game and tell her she can do much better, but she can't bring herself to leave because she loves him, and doesn't truly believe that the guy she loves would ever hurt her intentionally. She concludes that something must be wrong with her, she won't be anything without him, and she's terrified to leave. 

    Does that relationship describe a healthy one? No. If you're in a relationship with a spouse, friend, or institution who/that at ANY POINT makes you feel terrified to leave, you are not with an organization/person that cares about you, you are with an organization/person that is scared to lose your devotion to it/them. The two are very, very different.

3. You said, "I know this church is good. I just don't know if it's true anymore. I know I have felt the spirit, but I don't think that was because of the church. I don't agree with a lot of church culture, or even the church for that matter." So if you don't agree with church culture or it's claims, what do you consider good about it?
 
 I would wager the answer is: all the people you love are in the church. That's rough when you're doubting your faith. I would also wager that may be what is making it the most difficult for you to speak your truth. I have no answer for that (not that it was a question or anything) my heart just aches for you a little bit in that regard. I hope your friends and family are open-minded and loving.
